background.definition: Sepsis is a rapidly progressive spectrum of host response to infection that includes immune, inflammatory, and coagulation responses. It is an infectious subset of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). The very cytokine cascade that fights the causative infection becomes damaging to multiple organ systems and is frequently fatal. Sepsis was defined by the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3) as “life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection.” Additionally, the task force defined septic shock as "a subset of sepsis in which particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities are associated with a greater risk of mortality than with sepsis alone."

list.listitem: There are greater than 1.7 million cases of sepsis per year in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), more than 350,000 adults who are diagnosed with sepsis die in the hospital or get discharged to hospice.
Sepsis accounts for 10% of all ICU admissions.
Gram-negative bacteria were the predominant cause of septic shock in the past, but as of 1987 Gram-positive organisms have become the most common (57% vs. 37% for Gram-negative in year 2000).

Fungal infections causing sepsis rose by greater than 200% in the last 2 decades. They are more common in the immunocompromised, those treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and those with vascular catheters. Candidal species are the most common etiologic agent.
Bacterial cell wall components [most well established is lipopolysaccharide (LPS), from Gram-negative bacteria] activate antigen-presenting cells and lead to massive release of cytokines.
Cytokines involved include interleukins (IL-1, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), platelet-activating factor, endorphins, and nitric oxide.
Cytokines lead to vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, coagulability, fibrinolysis, and apoptosis.
Sepsis also involves both pro and anti-inflammatory responses, as well as cardiovascular, autonomic, hormonal, metabolic, and coagulation pathways.
Diagnose sepsis in adults with life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection. C
Do not rely solely on qSOFA, compared to SIRS, NEWS, or MEWS, as screening tool for sepsis or septic shock since it lacks diagnostic precision. A

Suspect sepsis in adults with likely clinical infection and at least two of the following: altered mental status, a respiratory rate of ≥22/minute, and a systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg (the qSOFA score). Confirmation of organ dysfunction using a SOFA score of 2 or higher is highly suggestive of sepsis. B

Diagnose septic shock in patients with sepsis who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, present with a serum lactate >2 mmol/L and require vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mm Hg. C
Check serum lactate in patients suspected of sepsis but do not rely on it for definitive diagnosis given its poor diagnostic accuracy. B
Consider alternative diagnoses for and continuously reevaluate patients with suspected sepsis or septic shock without confirmed infection. C

The Sepsis-3 consensus conference defines sepsis as "life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection." The task force recommends a bedside screening tool, the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA score), which includes altered mental status, a respiratory rate of 22 or greater per minute, and a systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or less. Patients suspected of having a clinical infection meeting at least 2 out of the 3 criteria are at high risk of poor outcomes.

It was recommended that these patients have the SOFA score calculated, and those with evidence of organ dysfunction and a SOFA score of 2 or more points be diagnosed with sepsis. SOFA score more than 2 carries a 10% in-hospital mortality.

Patients with sepsis who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, demonstrate a serum lactate level >2 mmol/L and who require vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg should be diagnosed with septic shock.
Patients with sepsis typically present with fever, hypotension, tachypnea, and tachycardia.

Shaking and chills are a highly specific but less sensitive predictor for bacteremia. Blood cultures and early initiation of antibiotics should be considered for patients with an episode of shaking and chills; lack of these subjective symptoms should not lead to the exclusion of bacteremia and early antibiotic treatment. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies with a total of 14,641 patients showed that the sensitivity and specificity of shaking chills were relatively modest at 37% (95% CI, 29% to 45%) and 87% (95% CI, 83% to 90%), respectively.

Any patient with a suspected clinical infection with at least 2 items from the qSOFA score (altered mental status, respiratory rate ≥22/minute, and a systolic blood pressure ≤100 mm Hg) should be suspected of having sepsis. If they have evidence of organ dysfunction as demonstrated by a SOFA score of 2 or more, sepsis can be diagnosed.
Blood cultures (at least 1 of 2 positive) have a very high sensitivity and specificity for identifying infection.

Serum lactate level >2 mmol/L suggests hypoperfusion and should be measured at initial presentation to risk stratify for aggressiveness of resuscitation. It is one of the components of the definition of septic shock, which also involves needing pressors to maintain a MAP ≥65 mm Hg.
Point-of-care lactate testing has not been demonstrated effective in improving outcomes, based on poor quality evidence.

Random cortisol levels may be useful only in cases of absolute adrenal insufficiency, but they have not been shown to be useful in septic shock patients with inadequate stress response due to relative adrenal insufficiency.
Sedimentation rate is not a sensitive test for sepsis. However, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) >100 is specific for serious infection.
Current guidelines do not advocate use of inflammatory markers (IL-6 or CRP) in the diagnosis of sepsis.

Procalcitonin is not reliable in distinguishing infectious from noninfectious causes of SIRS in critically ill adults. Hence, do not use procalcitonin to determine appropriateness of starting antimicrobial therapy. Consider using procalcitonin measurement for the deescalation of antibiotics in patients with septic shock; however it is not recommended for patients on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).

An elevated lactate to albumin ratio (LAR) is associated with poor prognosis. A retrospective observational study showed that LAR had an AUROC of 0.72 for 28 day mortality, compared to 0.67 for the SOFA score. Patients with sepsis and a LAR > 1.52 had a 3.8-fold higher risk of 28-day mortality, while those with a SOFA score >7 .5 had an approximately 2.7-fold higher risk of 28-day mortality.

Previous studies have suggested that the CRP to albumin ratio (CAR) and the procalcitonin (PCT) to albumin ratio (PAR) are associated with infection severity during the acute phase and can be used as prognostic predictors for sepsis mortality. Nonetheless, comparative studies on the predictive performance of each factor are insufficient.

A study identified 1477 adults with qSOFA >= 1, 29% of whom developed sepsis. Procalcitonin had the best accuracy for identifying patients who would develop sepsis within 96 hours (AUC 0.86, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.87), and was significantly better than adrenomedullin, CRP, pre-proadrenomedullin, and its cleavage products. Adding those markers to procalcitonin provided no better accuracy. Procalcitonin had positive and negative likelihood ratios of 3.8 and 031 at a cutoff of >= 0.5 mcg/L, and 6.2 and 0.4 at a cutoff of >= 0.25 mcg/L. In this population, the negative predictive value was 89% using the < 0.25 mcg/L cutoff, and the positive predictive value was 72% using the >= 0.5 mcg/L cutoff.

Noninvasive blood pressure monitoring using an automated cuff appears as safe as invasive blood pressure monitoring using an arterial line in terms of 28-day mortality for critically ill patients with shock, based on a multicenter RCT (n = 1,010). About 85% of the noninvasive group avoided insertion of an arterial line. Secondary outcomes were similar between groups (i.e., 90-day mortality, duration of ICU stay, need for renal replacement therapy, number of ventilator-free days). In terms of adverse events, the noninvasive group reported more pain from the automated cuff, while the invasive group had more hematoma and hemorrhage at the insertion site of the arterial line. Similarly, a case control study (n = 326) did not find improved survival using invasive blood pressure monitoring compared to noninvasive monitoring for critically ill patients with sepsis.

A study compared the prognostic value of several simple risk scores for patients with sepsis. The SOFA and LODS risk scores (AUC 0.74 to 0.75) were more accurate than the qSOFA and SIRS risk scores (AUC 0.64 to 0.66) for prediction of in-hospital mortality among ICU patients.
Among non-ICU patients, the qSOFA, SIRS, and SOFA were all similarly accurate for the prediction of in-hospital mortality.

Use the qSOFA score (2+ items) to identify patients with suspected infection who may have sepsis. Then, calculate the SOFA score (2 or higher) to diagnose sepsis. Patients who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, have a serum lactate > 2 mmol/L and who need pressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg are defined as having septic shock.
Appropriate cultures must be obtained before antibiotics are initiated. At least two blood cultures should be drawn, one percutaneously and one through every vascular access device present.

Cultures of urine, CSF, wounds, sputum, or other fluids should be taken as directed by the patient's presentation. Cultures should be obtained broadly if there is no obvious source from history and physical exam.

Screening in pregnancy. For admissions early in pregnancy and more than 3 days postpartum, non-pregnancy-adjusted sepsis screening tools performed better than pregnancy-adjusted tools. From 20 weeks of gestation through up to 3 days postpartum, using a pregnancy-adjusted sepsis screening tool increased sensitivity and minimized false-positive rates. The overall false-positive rate remained high.

Do not use procalcitonin to determine appropriateness of starting antimicrobials. However, procalcitonin may be helpful in guiding cessation of antimicrobial therapy after achieving source control if there remains uncertainty with clinical exam alone. B

When using beta-lactams, prolonged infusions (after initial bolus) appear superior to conventional intermittent infusions (<= 30 minutes), as they reduce short-term mortality based on two meta-analyses. A

Aim for an initial mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 65 mmHg instead of higher targets for adult patients with septic shock on vasopressors, and consider aiming for a MAP above 60 mmHg for patients above the age of 65 years. A
Use norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor. A Other options include vasopressin, A epinephrine, B selepressin, B and angiotensin II. C
Consider systemic corticosteroids for patients with septic shock with continued need for vasopressors. A
Do not use polymyxin B hemoperfusion, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), or vitamin C. B
Unless contraindicated, consider pharmacologic venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis for those at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding. B

Antibiotic therapy should be initiated in the first hour after cultures are drawn. Initial antibiotics should be broad spectrum to cover the suspected source of infection and should be reevaluated after 48 to 72 hours of therapy. They should be continued for 7 to 10 days, based on the patient's clinical response.

Do not use procalcitonin to determine appropriateness of starting antimicrobials. However, procalcitonin may be helpful in guiding cessation of antimicrobial therapy after achieving source control if there remains uncertainty based on the clinical exam alone.

A meta-analysis found that a beta lactam alone was as effective as beta lactam plus aminoglycoside in immunocompetent patients with sepsis.A Cochrane review confirmed this finding and found that combination treatment increased nephrotoxicity while all-cause mortality remained the same.
Consider adding antimicrobial coverage for MRSA for patients who are diagnosed with sepsis or septic shock and are high risk for MRSA.

When using beta-lactams, prolonged infusions (after initial bolus) appear superior to conventional intermittent infusions (<= 30 minutes), as they may reduce short-term mortality based on two meta-analyses. Differences in adverse events between the two approaches have not been reported, and prolonged infusion may be challenging in resource-limited settings.

A large multinational RCT (n = 7,031) of critically ill patients with sepsis found comparable 90-day mortality for continuous infusion and intermittent infusion of beta-lactam antibiotics. However, continuous infusion appears to increase clinical cure rate at 14 days (OR 1.26; CI 1.15-1.38; P<.001). In contrast, a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs, including this study, concluded that continuous infusion of beta-lactam antibiotics decreases 90-day mortality (pooled estimated RR 0.86; CI 0.72-0.98), lowers ICU mortality (RR 0.84; 0.70-0.97), and increases clinical cure (RR 1.16; 1.07-1.31). However, the included trials had varying definitions of sepsis, antibiotic choice, infusion time, and time to follow-up.

A retrospective study in a single tertiary hospital found a 5% higher mortality risk using the empiric treatment combination of vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam compared to vancomycin plus cefepime for adults with sepsis without a specific indication for anti-anaerobic antibiotic therapy.

Based on a multicenter international RCT (n = 3,608), 7 days of antibiotics appears as effective and safe as a 14 day antibiotic course for non-Staph aureus bacteremia in immunocompetent patients. subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis (n = 3,729), which included this trial, similarly concluded that 7 days of antibiotics was noninferior to 14 days of therapy for hospitalized patients with uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteremia, based on high-certainty evidence.

A cohort study of 18,000 patients using data from the Michigan Hospital Medicine Safety Consortium evaluating hospitalized patients with uncomplicated community-onset sepsis found that de-escalation from anti-MRSA and anti-pseudomonal antibiotics on day 4, compared to continuous broad-spectrum coverage, leads to less antibiotic exposure, shorter length of stay, and similar mortality.

Consider alternative diagnoses for and continuously reevaluate patients with suspected sepsis or septic shock without confirmed infection; discontinue empiric antibiotics once alternative etiology is confirmed or strongly favored.

Vasopressors should be added when patients continue to have hypotension or organ hypoperfusion after fluid resuscitation. Use norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor. Second-line options include vasopressin and its analogues, phenylephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, and angiotensin ll.

In a systematic review, norepinephrine demonstrated a mortality benefit with an absolute risk reduction of 11% and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 9, when compared to dopamine, primarily due to lower risk of arrhythmias with norepinephrine. Dopamine at higher doses has alpha-1 and beta-1 adrenergic properties, which will assist with vasoconstriction and increasing systemic vascular resistance, at the expense of also increasing the risk for cardiac arrhythmias.

Aim for an initial MAP of 65 mm Hg instead of higher targets for adult patients with septic shock on vasopressors. Higher MAP targets (80-85 mm Hg) vs. the traditional 65 mm Hg for initial resuscitation do not appear to reduce mortality.

For patients with septic shock who are being treated with norepinephrine with inadequate MAP, consider adding vasopressin for additional vasopressor support as opposed to escalating the dose of norepinephrine.

Vasopressin may be considered as add-on vasopressor if patients remain hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation and first-line pressor agents; infusion within 6 hours of septic shock reduced use of renal replacement therapy (RRT) in a meta-analysis. Angiotensin II was demonstrated to increase blood pressure in vasodilatory septic shock resistant to vasopressors in a single industry-sponsored concealed allocation trial.
Consider systemic corticosteroids for patients with septic shock with continued need for vasopressors.

3 systematic reviews of corticosteroid studies found low- to moderate-certainty evidence supporting a reduction in 28-day, 90-day, and hospital mortality with systemic corticosteroids, as well as low-certainty evidence suggesting shortening of ICU and hospital length of stay. Systemic steroids do not appear to significantly increase the risk of infection, but its effects on mucle weakness is uncertain. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence for continuous versus intermittent bolus administration of systemic steroids. A well-designed RCT (CORTICUS study) found that IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day did not reduce mortality. An updated trial in 2018 (ADRENAL trial) showed that, in patients with septic shock on mechanical ventilation receiving vasopressors, one week of hydrocortisone 200 mg/day did not reduce 90-day mortality but may be associated with shorter time until reversal of shock, shorter time to extubation, shorter length of stay in the ICU and less need for blood transfusions.

The Society of Critical Care Medicine released an update on the 2024 guidelines on the use of corticosteroids in sepsis, adult respiratory distress syndrome, and community acquired pneumonia. It is thought that corticosteroids may reduce hospital and long term mortality (defined as 60 days to 1 year) (RR 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89 - 1.00, low certainty) in patients with sepsis or septic shock. It has shown to reduce ICU and short term mortality (defined as 14-30 days) (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.88-0.98, moderate certainty) in patients with sepsis or septic shock. The 2024 update suggest to add corticosteroids to adult patients with septic shock (low certainty evidence) and recommend against adding high dose corticosteroids for short durations (hydrocortisone 400 mg per day for less than 3 days) for adult patients with septic shock. The proposed regimen for corticosteroids in the setting of septic shock is hydrocortisone 200 mg IV per day (continuously or divided every 6 hours) with or without fludrocortisone 50 mcg enterally for 7 days or until ICU discharge. A systematic review and meta analysis was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of combination therapy with fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone versus placebo or hydrocortisone alone. The analysis included 7688 patients, which showed a 15% reduction in all cause mortality with combination therapy (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.72, 0.99). When the combination therapy was compared to monotherapy with hydrocortisone, it was associated with a 12% lower risk of all cause mortality (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.74-1.03), however the results were not statistically significant. For patients with sepsis in the setting of severe community acquired pneumonia, it is recommended to administer corticosteroids (the regimen may be found in the "Pneumonia (community acquired) chapter).
Unless contraindicated, consider pharmacologic venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis and stress ulcer prophylaxis for those at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding.
Inotropic agents may be indicated if there is evidence of low cardiac output and refractory hypotension despite above strategies.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 RCTs found the use of dexmedetomidine in sepsis could significantly reduce mortality when compared to other sedatives such as benzodiazepines but not with propofol. Additionally, dexmedetomidine has the potential to decrease the inflammatory response in patients with sepsis when compared to other sedatives. Although it is known that dexmedetomidine can potentially bring on arrhythmias, the overall safety profile of the drug did not demonstrate a significant difference in the incidence of total adverse events.

An RCT found that recombinant activated protein C prevents 1 death for every 16 patients with septic shock who are treated.However, a systematic review of 5 studies with 5101 patients with severe sepsis did not find overall evidence of mortality benefit, and a more recent RCT also found no benefit of recombinant activated protein C on mortality.
Polyclonal intravenous immunoglobulin does not reduce mortality in adults with sepsis.
In a multicenter U.S. placebo-controlled RCT, the combination of vitamin C, corticosteroids, and thiamine did not improve SOFA scores in the 72 hours after administration.
A systematic review of 10 RCTs (n = 1400) found that IV vitamin C supplementation was associated with improved SOFA scores but no overall differences in patient-oriented outcomes.
A meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found no benefit of IV thiamine over placebo.
Do not use polymyxin B hemoperfusion for patients with sepsis or septic shock.

Previous studies have identified that lower total cholesterol, HDL and LDL levels were associated with poorer outcomes in patients with sepsis and septic shock. A small phase II trial of lipid emulsion therapy enrolled 49 patients and found no difference in SOFA scores between the two groups (p = 0.46).
Every patient should be evaluated for potential removal of infected source (eg, abscess drainage, wound debridement, or vascular device removal).

The Surviving Sepsis guidelines of 2021 mentioned, “For adults with sepsis or septic shock, we recommend rapidly identifying or excluding a specific anatomical diagnosis of infection that requires emergent source control and implementing any required source control intervention as soon as medically and logistically practical.”

Additionally, adults diagnosed with sepsis or septic shock, urgent removal of intravascular access devices that are suspected to be the source of infection is warranted as soon as another vascular access has been established.

Early goal-directed therapy, a protocol to reverse rapidly the hypoperfusion and lactate production resulting from sepsis, had been widely recommended based on preliminary studies. However, when compared to usual care in a well-designed, large RCT it does not decrease mortality and results in longer ICU stays and higher overall costs.

Consider initial fluid resuscitation at a rate of 30 mL/kg using balanced crystalloids within the first 3 hours for patients with septic shock or sepsis-induced hypoperfusion. There is no evidence for superiority of either crystalloids or colloids.

Two meta-analyses published in 2022 showed mortality benefit of using balanced crystalloids when compared to normal saline. A systematic review evaluating 13 RCTs found that the estimated effect of using balanced crystalloids versus normal saline in critically ill adults ranges from a 9% relative risk reduction to a 1% relative increase in the risk of death. Another systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating 15 RCTs found that in patients admitted with sepsis there was an overall relative risk reduction of 12% in mortality when balanced crystalloids were used when compared to normal saline, 13% relative risk reduction of 30-day mortality and 15% relative risk reduction of acute kidney injury. However, the results did not show a difference between balanced crystalloid versus normal saline when measured against 90-day mortality, need for RRT, and ICU length of stay.

In contrast, a Cochrane review found high-certainty evidence that there is no difference with regards to in-hospital mortality between balanced/buffered solutions (eg, lactated Ringers, Plasma-Lyte A, etc.) and 0.9% (normal, physiologic) saline for fluid resuscitation of critically ill adult patients. Low-certainty evidence demonstrates comparable outcomes between the two for preventing acute kidney injury. In terms of disease-oriented outcomes, very low-certainty evidence suggests less hyperchloremia, higher bicarbonate levels, and higher pH for critically ill patients treated with balanced solutions.

A multicenter European RCT of ICU patients with septic shock found that a restrictive intravenous fluid strategy did not affect mortality or serious adverse events at 90 days compared with a standard intravenous fluid strategy. Additionally, a nonblinded multicenter superiority trial in the US evaluating early (within 4 hours) restrictive versus liberal fluid management for sepsis-induced hypotension also found no difference in 90-day mortality or serious adverse events between the two groups.
Consider normalization of elevated serum lactate and monitoring dynamic measures (over static measures or physical exam) to guide fluid resuscitation of septic patients.
Consider using capillary refill time as an adjunct to other perfusion measures to guide fluid resuscitation in patients with septic shock.
Consider high flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) over other non-invasive ventilatory modalities for patients with sepsis-induced hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Use low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg) over high tidal volume ventilation (>10 mL/kg) for patients with sepsis-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Compared to initiation of RRT after 48 hours, initiation of RRT within 12 hours of diagnosis of severe AKI in patients with septic shock did not improve 90-day mortality.

An RCT reported that 48 hours of external cooling to maintain body temperature between 36.5 and 37 degrees Celsius in patients with septic shock improved all-cause mortality compared to usual care (NNT = 7 at 14 days), although this study was not specifically designed to evaluate mortality.
Control of blood glucose ≤180 mg/dL is recommended in both sepsis and septic shock. Recent well-designed RCTs do not support the benefit of strict blood glucose control in ICU patients in general.
Consider restarting enteral nutrition within 72 hours for patients with sepsis or septic shock who can tolerate enteral feeding.
The Mortality in Emergency Department Sepsis Score (MEDS) is sepsis specific and was designed to risk stratify patients rapidly in the emergency room to facilitate early resuscitation (). B
The predictive value of the MEDS score for severity and 28-day mortality may be improved when combined with procalcitonin level. B
A vasopressin/norepinephrine ratio <0.001 predicts development of septic shock within 6 hours in patient with sepsis. C
An increase in SOFA score of at least 2 in an ICU patient and a qSOFA score of 2 or more in an ED patient are both better at predicting in-hospital mortality than the SIRS criteria. B
An increase in the qSOFA score for ED patients with or without suspected infection is associated with increased in-hospital mortality, higher rates of admission, and longer lengths of stay. B

Patient Characteristic Points Assigned
Predisposition
Age >65 years 3
Nursing home resident 2
Rapidly terminal comorbid illness 6
Infection
Lower respiratory infection 2
Response
Bands ?5% 3
Organ dysfunction
Tachypnea or hypoxemia 3
Septic shock 3
Platelet count <150,000/mm3 3
Altered mental status 2
Point Range MEDS Group 28-Day Predicted Mortality Rate
0-4 Very low 1.1%
5-7 Low 4.4%
8-12 Moderate 9.3%
13-15 High 16.1%
<15 Very high 39%
